# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by successive technological advances, from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and subsequently drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. Despite the remarkable efficacy of contemporary DES, concerns regarding permanent metallic implants—including chronic inflammation, impaired vasomotion, late stent thrombosis, and the inability to perform future surgical revascularization—motivated the development of bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) [2,3]. The conceptual appeal of BVS lies in providing transient mechanical support and antiproliferative drug delivery, followed by complete resorption that restores natural vessel physiology [4].

## Rationale and Device Design

The theoretical advantages of BVS include the restoration of vasomotor function, late luminal enlargement, plaque regression, and freedom from the lifelong risks associated with permanent implants [5,6]. The most extensively studied device, the Absorb everolimus-eluting bioresorbable scaffold (Abbott Vascular), was constructed from poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) with a poly-D,L-lactide coating eluting everolimus [7]. The PLLA backbone degrades through hydrolysis into lactic acid, ultimately metabolized via the Krebs cycle over approximately two to three years [8]. Early imaging studies using optical coherence tomography and intravascular ultrasound demonstrated favorable vessel healing and restoration of vasoreactivity [9,10].

## Early Clinical Evidence

The first-in-human ABSORB cohort A and B studies established proof of concept, demonstrating feasibility, acceptable acute performance, and progressive scaffold resorption with preserved luminal dimensions [11,12]. These encouraging results led to larger randomized trials comparing BVS with metallic DES [13]. The ABSORB II, ABSORB III, ABSORB Japan, and ABSORB China trials collectively enrolled thousands of patients and formed the principal evidence base for regulatory approval [14,15,16].

## Randomized Trial Outcomes

ABSORB III, the pivotal trial supporting U.S. approval, randomized 2008 patients and demonstrated non-inferiority of the Absorb BVS to the Xience cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent for target-lesion failure at one year [15]. However, longer-term follow-up revealed troubling signals. The ABSORB II trial, with three-year results, failed to demonstrate superiority in vasomotion and showed a higher rate of device-related events, including scaffold thrombosis [14,17]. Meta-analyses subsequently confirmed an increased risk of device thrombosis, particularly very late scaffold thrombosis occurring beyond one year [18,19].

A pooled patient-level analysis of randomized trials demonstrated significantly higher rates of target-lesion failure and scaffold thrombosis with BVS compared with metallic DES, especially between one and three years—the period coinciding with active scaffold resorption [20,21]. These findings were corroborated by registry data, including the GHOST-EU and AIDA studies, which reported real-world scaffold thrombosis rates exceeding expectations [22,23].

## Mechanisms of Failure

Several mechanisms contributed to adverse outcomes. The relatively thick struts (157 μm) of the Absorb device, compared with contemporary thin-strut DES, predisposed to flow disturbance and thrombogenicity [24]. Suboptimal implantation technique, including inadequate lesion preparation, undersizing, and insufficient post-dilatation, was strongly associated with adverse events [25]. Late strut discontinuity during resorption and scaffold dismantling could expose flow surfaces and precipitate thrombosis [26]. The importance of meticulous implantation—encapsulated in the "PSP" approach (adequate Preparation, appropriate Sizing, and high-pressure Post-dilatation)—became increasingly recognized [27].

## Market Withdrawal and Lessons Learned

In light of accumulating safety concerns and declining sales, Abbott withdrew the Absorb BVS from the commercial market in 2017 [28]. This represented a significant setback but yielded valuable lessons regarding device design, patient selection, and implantation technique. Importantly, the failure of the first-generation device did not invalidate the bioresorbable concept itself [29].

## Future Directions

Ongoing development focuses on next-generation scaffolds with thinner struts, improved mechanical properties, faster resorption kinetics, and alternative materials such as magnesium-based alloys [30]. The magnesium-based DREAMS/Magmaris scaffold and other novel polymeric devices aim to overcome the limitations of first-generation technology while preserving the physiological benefits of resorption [30]. Rigorous long-term randomized data, optimized implantation protocols, and careful patient selection will be essential before BVS can re-establish a role in routine practice.

## Conclusion

Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds represented an ambitious effort to transcend the limitations of permanent metallic implants. While first-generation devices ultimately failed to demonstrate sustained safety and efficacy, the experience generated profound insights into device engineering and procedural technique. The bioresorbable concept remains scientifically compelling, and continued innovation may yet deliver devices that fulfill the original promise of transient scaffolding with restoration of native vascular function.
